NORTH KOREA-STATEMENT RESPECTING SEIZURE OF U.S. SHIP
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on Friday last a number of questions were raised with regard to the serious situation which has developed as a result of the seizure of the United States ship known as Pueblo by North Korea and their continued detention of that United States naval vessel and its crew. It was suggested by the hon. member for Ontario that I should make a statement today.
I am sure all hon. members will understand that the fullest possible statement cannot be made at the present time because of the important discussions and consultations that are now still under way at the United Nations. The United States authorities have stated categorically that at the time of its seizure on the evening of January 21 the vessel in question was in international waters. We accept the United States statement with regard to the ship's co-ordinates at that time. The information available to us strongly indicates that this point does lie in international waters and not in territorial waters. North Korea has alleged otherwise but so far had not put forward any evidence in support of its contention.
The ship in question was under United States command and not under the command of the United Nations in Korea. The dispute therefore is essentially one between the United States and North Korea. We do not consider it to be a violation of the Korean armistice of 1953. Canada therefore on that account is not involved. However, we are concerned with the potential danger to international peace which this incident involves. We have a particular responsibility as a member of the Security Council to make every effort to find a peaceful solution.
On Thursday last when I was not in the house questions were asked about our obligations to Korea under the declaration made by the 16 contributing countries in the United Nations force. Canada's present obligations to
Korea derive from the 16-nation declaration on Korea issued at Washington on July 27, 1953 immediately following the signing of the Korean armistice agreement. That declaration includes this statement:
We affirm, in the interests of world peace, that if there is a renewal of the armed attack, challenging again the principles of the United Nations, we should again be united and prompt to resist.
The United Nations command remains in Korea with the full sanction and authority of the Security Council. Canada still has a liaison officer attached to the United Nations command but the last of the Canadian contingent, which was the third largest national force sent to Korea as a result of the Security Council's appeal in 1950, was withdrawn in 1957, four years after the conclusion of the Korean armistice agreement.
[DOT] (2:40 p.m.)
There is not at this time any specific Canadian commitment to supply military forces or equipment. Should the situation in Korea develop adversely, and I sincerely hope it will not-it is certainly a matter of concern that there has been in recent months a marked increase in the number of incidents investigated by North Korea-it would be for the Canadian government and parliament, in the absence of a new United Nations resolution, to decide whether the situation fell within the meaning of the 16-nation declaration of which this country is a signatory. In any event the matter would have to be referred to the Security Council before any action could be taken by the United Nations.
The Security Council met on January 26 at the request of the United States. The Canadian representative, noting the council's primary responsibility for international peace and security, supported inscription of an item on the increase of tension in the area of Korea and welcomed the decision of the United States to seek the assistance of the United Nations to help it solve a difficult problem through diplomatic channels. Our ambassador suggested that one possible way of bringing about a speedy and equitable solution might be an arrangement for an intermediary or intermediaries.

Seizure of U.S. Ship Pueblo
At a second meeting of the council on Saturday there was unanimous support for the further Canadian suggestion that progress might best be achieved by private consultations which would enable members of the council to consider and develop any ideas or suggestions they might have. This seemed to be the best way of dealing with the immediate problem of the Pueblo.
Those consultations, in which all members of the council have been participating, have been proceeding over the week end in New York and in a number of national capitals. They proceeded this morning, and they are taking place again at this very moment. A number of ideas have been explored I think in a useful and constructive fashion. I am encouraged to date by the sense of responsibility and restraint, as well as by the sense of urgency, which have marked these consultations. I must say that the government of the United States has displayed moderation and a commendable desire to seek a solution through diplomatic means. I hope all countries which may be involved in the consequences of failure to resolve the controversy will show an equal determination to seek a settlement through peaceful means.
Furthermore, members of the Security Council, and this includes Canada, have a special responsibility to seek a reasonable and early solution. I can assure the house that the government is following this matter very closely, is in continuous contact with the parties concerned, and I hope the end result of these consultations will be the resolving of this matter in a way which will not add to the dangers in the situation.

So I think we have a particular responsibility not only to do what can be done in the interests of international peace, not only to discharge our responsibilities as a member of the Security Council, but also in view of our own situation as a signatory of the armistice. Mr. Speaker, I am sure members of the house will welcome the statement by the Secretary of State for External Affairs. I think we should look upon it as very commendable that a great power like the United States should have referred this serious incident to the United Nations rather than taking unilateral military action which could have far reaching consequences for the peace of the world.
It seems to me that from Canada's viewpoint there are two main points to be underscored. The first is that we do not look upon this incident of the seizure of the United States ship Pueblo as a violation of the North Korean armistice of 1953. I think we have to see this incident in the context of the cold war and the long series of incidents that have
January 29, 1968

arisen out of espionage and counter-intelligence carried on by both ships and planes. There have been many of these instances over the past few years, and this is simply another one of them.
[DOT] (2:50 p.m.)
I am glad the Secretary of State for External Affairs has made a clear declaration with respect to Canada's position. I noticed that last Friday the United States state department called together the diplomatic representatives of the 16 countries which were signatories to the Korean armistice agreement. Although that meeting may have been called merely for the dissemination of information, in the light of some of the statements that have been made by congressional leaders in the United States to the effect that their country was still at war with North Korea, and that if hostilities were resumed it might be necessary to use tactical nuclear weapons, I think it is imperative for Canada at this time to make abundantly clear that we do not regard the Pueblo incident as a resumption of hostilities in North Korea, and that consequently Canada has no military obligation.
The second point that must be understood is that the immediate task is to secure the return of the ship and its crew to the United States. I do not think there is any value in arguing now about the location of the ship. This is something that will have to be determined by some international body or some intermediary. The United States claimed that the ship was 25 miles from the mainland, and later set the figure at 15.4 miles from the Korean island of Ungdo. North Korea claims that the ship was 7.6 miles from the mainland and was in its territorial waters.
I think the most pressing problem is to secure the services of an intermediary acceptable to both sides who can try to find a solution under which the ship and its crew can be returned. Later, if it were found there was some invasion of territorial waters, whatever indemnification is necessary could be set at that time. The difficulty will be in securing an intermediary who is acceptable to both sides to be appointed by the United Nations, in view of the fact that North Korea is not a member of the United Nations.
I hope the Secretary of State for External Affairs is giving some thought to the possibility of using the neutral supervisory commission, which was accepted by both sides on July 27, 1953 and which might now be acceptable to both sides as an intermediary. I think this incident points up the necessity of having
Seizure of U.S. Ship Pueblo established at the United Nations some type of international tribunal which can ascertain the accuracy of facts in a dispute of this nature and report these facts to the Security Council.
I think the minister and our representative at the United Nations are to be commended for the contribution they have already made in pressing for an intermediary who will be acceptable to both sides, but I think the important thing at this stage is for the government to make it abundantly clear that this isolated incident, regrettable though it may be, cannot be looked upon by Canada as a violation of the Korean armistice agreement and that it does not involve Canada in any military commitments.

Mr. Speaker, I wish to join with the members of the opposition to congratulate the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Martin). We think that he displayed great wisdom until now, for this is a special case. Indeed, it is in similar circumstances that world wars often break out and the minister knows that perfectly well.
Not only is it our duty to see to it that the 1963 treaty is not violated by either country, but also to bring out the truth, in order to give justice to both parties.
Nevertheless, we find it rather strange

and I think that will be the stumbling-block for the United Nations, which will probably have to settle the question-that only one party, the United States, is represented at the United Nations, since the other party, North Korea, is not a member of the organization and therefore will probably not be present to defend itself.
But the first thing that strikes us, we who are not military men, is to hear that a spy ship was navigating in either territorial or international waters, and the crucial question will be to determine the location of the ship. The United States, naturally, will say that it was in international waters, and North Korea will maintain that it was in her territorial waters. I think it will be rather difficult to get at the truth, because only the crew of the American ship really knows where the ship was.
Allowances will have to be made but, once again, the Secretary of State for External Affairs was very prudent. We must be increasingly careful because, while we want

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it seems that the degree of co-operation between the federal and provincial governments reaches its zenith when somebody desires to take away Indian rights. This is what happened in 1943 when the British Columbia Indian Reserves Mineral Resources Act was passed by this parliament as a result of an agreement entered into between the province of British Columbia and the government of Canada without consultation with or the advice of our native Indian people.
One provision of the act requires that the native Indian people must surrender, in other words give up, their entitlement to mineral resources on the reserves before these resources can be exploited and developed. This is an obstacle in the way of any such development and this bill seeks to remove it by repealing the act itself.

The house resumed, from Friday, January 26, consideration in committee of Bill No. C-163, to implement a broadcasting policy for Canada, to amend the Radio Act in consequence thereof and to enact other consequential and related provisions-Miss LaMarsh- Mr. Batten in the chair.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
When the committee rose on Friday clause 2 (g) (i) was under consideration, with an amendment proposed by the hon. member for Red Deer. Clause 2 (c) was allowed to stand.
On clause 2-Broadcasting policy jor Canada.

Mr. Chairman, at the close of the debate last Friday on Bill C-163 I moved an amendment to clause 2 (g) (i). I did so because I am convinced that if this bill is to be of any use to the management of the C.B.C. and if it is to give us any assurance that the management in relation particularly

DEBATES	January 29, 1968
to programming, will be more effective than it has been under the former arrangement it is necessary that guide lines be laid down in a more effective way than is the case with those already in existence. It may seem that the amendment is a very minor one and does not in any way really change the intent of this clause, but I believe it is important because it lays down a guide line that is vital to the well-being of this country. During this debate I have spoken as a parent concerned about what is being presented over our public broadcasting system that may be damaging to family life and the welfare of our youth in an age which has more pressures and temptations than ever before.
The amendment deserves to be given very serious consideration by the minister. It also certainly deserves the support of the members of this house who I believe are just as concerned as I am about the environment in which young people generally and our own children find themselves today. Television can be a tremendous force for good if it sets objectives directed toward supporting that aspect of our society which is vital to the future of our country. There is no more important aspect than home and family life. It is my belief that the public broadcasting system has a greater and more real responsibility to the parents, families and young people of this country than perhaps even our educational institutions, and I do not detract from their responsibility in any way. Certainly television, if it faces up to its responsibility in this area, could be a tremendous force for good, and it is in this light that television management should view its responsibility.
Many of my constituents and others from all provinces of Canada who have written me are concerned that, unfortunately, the C.B.C., our public broadcasting system, is producing the opposite effect in its television broadcasts. It would seem, as many of these letters suggest, that there must be some people who are intentionally and deliberately attempting to break down our culture and the concept of family life in this country. Otherwise the type of programming we now have could not continue as it does.
The second part of the amendment might be considered from the aspect of whether programs disseminated over our public broadcasting system can be considered as encouraging criminal activity. That is a pretty serious statement to make but I am convinced that is exactly what is happening. No better evidence of this could be provided than the
January 29, 1968
program last night relating to the drug culture. I do not know how many saw it. At first it did not seem to me to be such a bad presentation. As I studied it and made note of some of the remarks and what seemed to be the over-all objective, I could come to no other conclusion but that it was not a public affairs show and not entertainment but a very subtle and clever job of selling drugs as an acceptable part of the new morality. This program was thoroughly advertised to ensure a very large audience. I am sure the majority of those who watched it were teenage university and high school students.
An lion. Member: When was it shown?

It was shown on the C.B.C. program "The Way It Is" between ten and eleven o'clock p.m., Sunday, January 28.
I am so concerned about this drug culture program shown on C.B.C., after weeks of advertising to ensure a large audience, that I feel it can only be termed the greatest betrayal of Canadian youth and the most potentially dangerous emanation from any broadcasting agency ever to be seen in Canada. The tragedy is that almost no adults watching it would understand the dangers.
Except the hon. member, no doubt.

I am convinced that I was not the only one who recognized the dangers. As a result of the telephone calls and telegrams I received this morning I realize there are thousands of parents across this country who agree with me.
It seems to me that Ross McLean, the producer of "Drug Culture", and Patrick Watson deliberately attempted to encourage the teenage population to take up the use of drugs. To understand the show you have to put yourself in the place of a Canadian or American teenager watching it. Young people in cities and towns all know of some of their friends who have tried drugs, or have heard of someone who has, particularly around the schools and colleges. In fact, I have a personal friend whose daughter attends a high school in western Canada and just last week she was approached by drug pushers right in the high school where she attends classes.
[DOT] (3:50 p.m.)
Did you report it to the police?

Therefore there is a temptation to try these drugs. We have all
6075
Canadian Policy on Broadcasting experienced that young, impressionable period of life and we should know that such things appeal because they are different and unknown. What could this program do for the youth who watched it except encourage them to experiment with drugs?
Not even one, strong statement was made about the danger of taking drugs. The one person on the panel who opposed it was an old man whose statements were for the most part all right but were anything but forceful. I ask hon. members to listen to what a leading medical man has to say, as quoted in today's Globe and Mail. "L.s.d. is a desperately dangerous drug", said Dr. J. S. Prichard, chief of neurology at the Hospital for Sick Children. Then he said:
Enough evidence is in now that youngsters shouldn't even take one dose-and I'm not talking about the legal or moral aspects, but about the physical.
Later he referred to the evidence that l.s.d. causes breaks in the chromosomes which carry the genes that transmit hereditary characteristics and also govern certain processes within the body. He said there have also been reports of psychoses, that is, severe mental illnesses, resulting from the use of l.s.d.
On the program last night there was not one single reference to the adverse effects of using drugs. The producers of the program attempted to encourage their use and to give the impression that the taking of them was not really harmful. "Enough evidence is in now", said Dr. Prichard, "that youngsters shouldn't even take one dose." He referred to other scientific evidence to support his statement. These statements were made in the course of a seminar for teachers. Last week a statement attributed to the department of health of New York city revealed that in that city there are at the present time at least 150 young people who are in mental institutions as a result of taking l.s.d.
I have in my hand a quotation from an issue of the New York Times published only a few months ago. One of the world's authorities on the use of drugs, when speaking at the University of California, Los Angeles, Dr. Constandinos J. Miras, a pharmacologist from the University of Athens, said that chronic users of marijuana usually suffer adverse personality changes and are subject to damage to the brain and other organs. Dr. Miras said, further:
I can recognize a chronic marijuana user from afar by the way he walks, talks and acts.

This newspaper article continues:
He said personality changes alter use of the drug Included slowed speech, lethargy, lowered inhibitions and loss of morality. But users may also become suddenly violent without apparent provocation. They will even kill," Dr. Miras said. The common medical belief is that marijuana is not harmful to health.
That was the idea that was put across in the program last night, without any mention of the statements by health authorities. Dr. Miras went on to say that these symptoms occur after only two cigarettes a day for two years or longer. He said that personality changes result.
I can only add to these reports that I know that in California tragic numbers of people have been drawn into the use of heroin and other drugs by starting on marijuana, and most of them started on marijuana while attending educational institutions. Look at the police records in the United States and see how many of their young criminals had their moral level lowered by marijuana and entered upon crime without a moral qualm as a result, it is believed, of using the drug.
I say; Wake up Canada. There are men in the C.B.C. who would betray this country. Any research of any consequence at all would have turned up these facts for the producers of "The Way It Is" if they had been interested in presenting the other side of the story. Any responsible producer would have put these facts in their proper perspective on that show last night. But what did we see? No strong voices were opposed to the misuse of these drugs. There was only subtle discussion giving the pros and cons in a very calm and deliberate way.
It is obvious that the producers of this show deliberately selected their panelists, their audience and their film clips to play up the joys of drug-taking, making only a token reference to the dangers thereof. There was one short, quick sequence of a man writhing about in the withdrawal symptoms but minutes on end portraying good looking, intelligent boys talking about the fun, appeal and joyous effects of taking drugs. They are, in the words of one youth, king for a day.
This program last night even showed youth how to prepare the needle and how to prepare the powdered drug and put it into the needle. Then it showed where and how to inject it. Is this necessary on a public show which has the intention, or at least should have the intention, of showing the dangers of taking drugs? I do not think it is.

DEBATES	January 29, 1968
There was a bearded professor from Buffalo on the program who is at this very moment facing drug charges in the courts of the United States. He was brought to Canada to appear on a panel show that would give our young people the impression of promoting the use of drugs. This professor gave a long harangue on the virtues of the drug culture. Then an eloquent youth from the audience did likewise. He said, "What if only four or five die each year from l.s.d.? What is that compared with the millions killed in the war in Viet Nam? We in the drug culture are against war". Take drugs, was his message, and join the new generation who would save the world.
There was not one protest from that youthful audience against the use of drugs; there was only support. I know there are many responsible young people in our institutions and in our society who are opposed to the use of drugs and are protesting against the increasing traffic in drugs in our educational institutions. But where were their voices last night? They were not included, and it was not intended that they should be. If I were a member of the Mafia I would pay $1 million to promote a program such as we heard last night on "The Way It Is." Perhaps we had better look into that too. The sad thing is that most adults, as I did at first, would not even catch the subtle appeal that was intended to attract youth to accepting the message that drugs are okay. Try it, the youth implied, lots of kids do; there is no trouble getting out of it if you want to stop it afterwards.
I quote the words of the moderator of the program, Mr. Saywell, as I took them down, "We have come a long way from hostility to drugs to the investigation of them." So now mothers and fathers need not warn their children of the dangers of drugs; this question is being investigated to find out whether there is any harm in them. That was the gist of his remarks.
It is necessary to understand the appeal of television. It is not the words that matter so much as the appeal to the emotions. The camera played on the face of a beautiful boy several times for periods up to a minute while apparently he was under the influence of drugs. What a come-on for youth.
With regard to air pollution the C.B.C. portrayed on a feature program a few months ago, a spine-chilling spectacle of the tragic human consequences of fluoride polluted air. But with drugs there is no presentation. Instead there is a quiet approach showing that drugs are not really so bad after all.

It also implied that the use of these drugs should not be considered a criminal act.
I do not intend to speak much longer. I commend this amendment to the minister and to the committee as one which merely sets down some guide lines for management in controlling not only the technical and financial aspects of public broadcasting but also programming in relation to what is apparently the attitude today among many television producers that free speech gives them the right to use the airwaves to promote their

Not only must we ascertain that the taxpayers' money is well spent; it is also necessary to ensure that a program dealing with the drug problem or the drug culture, as it is called, is fair in its approach and attempts to present the other side of the picture, at least by giving the general impression that the use of drugs is wrong. Mr. Chairman, in speaking on the amendment, which I hope will be brought to a vote and disposed of very shortly, may I recall to the memories of hon. members something of the very long background of our deliberations on this legislation. When the legislation was introduced last year I believe I was one of the first to urge that it be sent as quickly as possible to the standing committee on broadcasting. I did this, as others did, because in considering as complex and detailed a matter as the one with which we are now concerned it is surely obvious that the standing committee, where all parties can be represented and where a detailed discussion can take place, is the best place in which to carry on an efficient examination of the legislation. We did get it to the committee and, as others have said earlier, we discussed it there for 12 days, clause by clause, paragraph by paragraph, and in some cases word by word. Not only were members of the broadcasting committee privileged to take part in the discussion but, as we all know, any hon. member who has an interest in the subject before a committee can come to the committee and speak on that point.
I believe that in some respects our consideration of the bill in committee was very similar to the earlier committee consideration and discussion of the white paper which preceded the legislation and was considered in committee for days and days. All these considerations followed very far reaching examinations by at least one important commission studying the broadcasting situation in Canada. After these deliberations and the detailed and largely impartial committee consideration have taken place, here we are back in the house where we have spent all of last week going over all these clauses very much as we did at the committee level. With these facts in mind I must admit I was wrong when I urged that the matter be sent to the committee for consideration because it has turned

6078	COMMONS
Canadian Policy on Broadcasting out that we might just as well have continued the discussion here in the house instead of sending the matter to the committee. In that way at least we would have avoided duplication of our discussions.
I imagine that in a matter such as broadcasting it is impossible to make much speed when we are considering clauses of this type because what should be broadcast is very largely a matter of personal opinion. As someone has said before me, broadcasting is rather like sex. A lot of it is not much good but it is all interesting. I think this quality of interest is what spurs some hon. members to discuss this matter. I believe that the length of the discussion we have had in committee of the whole house should now spur us to bring the amendment before us, and no doubt others which will follow, to a vote as soon as possible.
I remember when we were in the standing committee one hon. member remarked at the end of a tedious session, in which I think we made a change of one word in a subclause, that had Moses had the same problem with his legislation when he brought it down from above and gave it to the children of Israel and had he had the same orators to contend with in his organization as the ministers and others have here, the children of Israel would probably still be somewhere in the wilderness debating an amendment to a subclause on a point in the tenth commandment which is in part at least that it is wrong to covet thy neighbour's wife. No doubt the amendment would be to the effect that it would be all right to do so between the hours of 5 and 7 p.m., particularly if nothing came of it.
In speaking against the amendment-and I do not want to take up any more time of the house-I hope that in what I have said I do not appear in any way to be putting myself above any member of the house or of the broadcasting committee. I believe many other hon. members share the general views I have expressed on the need for making better progress. I would say there are three reasons therefore. First, Canada needs this legislation and has been waiting for it for a long time. Second. New officials in the public sector have been appointed and are waiting to receive the legislation in order to go to work to improve some of the matters about which hon. members have complained. Finally, the broadcasting situation, important as it is, is by no means the only major problem confronting the Canadian people at this time. So I sit down in the hope we will have an early

Mr. Chairman, I should like to speak on this amendment for a moment. I think the amendment proposed by the hon. member for Red Deer is unnecessary, particularly if we are to give import to the words "high standard". I cannot imagine a program being of high standard if it gives encouragement to criminal activity or if it does not help to safeguard sound family life. A program of high standard in which there is a free and frank discussion affecting family life cannot do anything else but achieve the objective sought by the hon. member in his amendment. We could put in a dozen clauses to cover the many worthy objectives and virtuous things we would like to see done. However, I believe these objectives are covered by the words "high standard", and we rather weaken the meaning of those words by trying to go in the direction the hon. member is suggesting.

Mr. Chairman, my remarks will be very brief in relation to the amendment proposed by the hon. member for Red Deer. I think there should be a little balance on the record in this regard. Everyone would not view the broadcast to which reference has been made in the same light as the hon. member did. The hon. member for Red Deer has very little faith in young people if he believes they are all automatically going to take drugs as a result of seeing the program.
Generally speaking, we found the program to be quite good and the panel discussion seemed to be good. I do not like these amendments that keep coming up which seem to impose more and more control all the time. I thought that the panel discussion part of the program was very useful, not only for the young people but for myself as a member of parliament. I was interested in listening to it because I know that later we will be discussing bills which bear upon the use of drugs in our country. I do not see the reason for all the alarms which have been sounded by the hon. member for Red Deer, and I am sure most members do not either.

Mr. Chairman, in rising to comment on the amendment proposed by the hon. member for Red Deer I should like to refer back to the discussion of this clause in the standing committee. You will find it reported in the official report of the committee for November 23, 1967. There are some questions and answers on page 109 of that issue, and I quote myself:
' Mr- Cowan: We are talking about clause 2(g) (i): "the national broadcasting service should (i) be a balanced service of information, enlightenment and entertainment for people of different ages, interests and tastes covering the whole range of programming in fair proportion."
I then asked the minister to tell us what a balance in fair proportion was in her opinion, and I will give her answer in a moment. I should like to point out that last week I gave two quotations from the minister's remarks when discussing C.A.T.V. I cited her remarks in the committee report for November 28, page 166, where she said:
I am not very familiar with the economics of them-
On page 167 of the same report she is reported as having said:
No, but of my knowledge I do not know that much detail about it.
Those are the two statements the minister made about C.A.T.V. I should like to read the statement she made on November 23 in connection with the clause we are discussing right now. I asked the minister to tell us what proportion of balance, in her opinion, was fair. This is the answer I received.
I believe that is a rhetorical question, Mr. Chairman.
It was not a rhetorical question but the minister gave me that snappy answer. That was her reply to a man who was seeking some information from her. I asked the minister to tell us what proportion of balance, in her opinion, would be fair. I then said:
Well, are these not rhetorical words in here?
The words to which I referred were:
-the national broadcasting service should be a balanced service of information, enlightenment and entertainment for people of different ages, interests and tastes covering the whole range of programming in fair proportion.
This is the snappy answer I got when I asked if these were not rhetorical words in the subclause. The Secretary of State, the person responsible to parliament for the
Canadian Policy on Broadcasting C.B.C. and the Board of Broadcast Governors, answered as follows as reported on page 109:
It is intended to mean exactly what it says; but I am not in a position to define what the individual words of it mean.
There is an answer for you if you ever got one, and it is contained in an official government report of the proceedings of this committee whose work the hon. member for New Westminster has been extolling. Talk about progress, when the minister responsible for this whole broadcasting field answers a question about the meaning of this clause now under discussion by saying "it is intended to mean exactly what it says, but I am not in a position to define what the individual words of it mean."
I went on to state:
The words were not chosen because they are so nebulous, were they?
The answer was "No." I then went on to point out what a balanced program is in the opinion of the C.B.C. and the Board of Broadcast Governors because I had with me at that committee meeting, as I have here in the House of Commons, a copy of the Fowler report of 1965. This report is looked upon evidently as the Bible of broadcasting by those in the television and broadcasting world. During the committee meeting I pointed out the following to the minister, who had advised me she did not know what the words meant but that they meant exactly what they said. As reported on page 109 of the committee report I said:
At the top of page 29 of the report of the committee on broadcasting 1985, you will find the following: B.B.G. program categories-all television stations (March 1-7, 1964) English language-C.B.C. owned and operated; information 37.5 per cent; light entertainment, 52.2 per cent. Would you call the light entertainment at 52.2 per cent a balanced or a fair proportion of the programming of the C.B.C.?
Here is another enlightening answer from the minister:
If you are asking for my personal opinion, of course, I can give it but I do not know that this helps the committee very much. My personal opinion on that is no more important than that of the other 20 million people in the country.
The Secretary of State, responsible for the C.B.C. and the Board of Broadcast Governors, informed the committee, and I am now advising the house, that her opinion was no more important than that of the other 20 million people in the country. Such humility is to be admired. However, I ask her to assume the

Canadian Policy on Broadcasting responsibilities that have been entrusted to her by the parliament of Canada. I then said: We have here figures showing the English C.B.C. giving 37.5 per cent to information-that is mentioned here in this section-52.2 per cent to entertainment; and for enlightenment-which, I presume, would include arts, letters and the sciences-2.2 per cent. Is this what you would call a balanced service and a fair proportion between information, enlightenment and entertainment, when the enlightenment brings us 2.2 per cent of the programs?
The minister's reply was:
Of course I do not agree that it is a balance.
Mr. Chairman and members of the committee, if you look at page 29 of this Bible of the Canadian broadcasting world, the Fowler report for 1965, you will find that all the English language stations in Canada, during the period March 1 to 7, 1964, devoted 34 per cent of time to information, 57 per cent to light entertainment and 1.6 per cent to the arts, letters and sciences. If any clause as nebulous as this ever needed amending, this one is it. The Secretary of State says she does not know what the words mean. When the hon. member for Red Deer stands up and tries to clarify the directions given to the C.B.C. and the new council on radio and television, then people say we should not be giving more directions to this organization than those contained in this most nebulous clause.
If you feel that the English language stations have been pretty light on enlightenment in devoting 1.6 per cent of their time to enlightenment, which means they devote 98.4 per cent to information and light entertainment, then look at the French language stations. These figures are contained on the same page 29 of the report. The French language television stations between March 1 and 7, 1964 devoted 32.9 per cent of their broadcasting time to information and 58.6 per cent to light entertainment. Evidently the French are more interested in enlightenment than the English sector. The English stations gave only 1.6 per cent of their time to enlightenment whereas the French stations topped that figure with a magnificent 1.7 per cent. This means that 0.1 per cent more time was given to enlightenment on the French networks than on the English.

The interesting thing about the English stations giving 34 per cent of their time and the French stations 32.9 per cent to information is this. I should like to know how much of this information is repetitive. Do they regard their

news broadcasts for five minutes every hour on the hour and for three minutes every half hour on the half hour as being information? If you were to listen, Mr. Chairman, to these news broadcasts over a period of 24 hours- and many newspaper publishers and newspaper people have done so over the years-you would find that the repetition of news items is nauseating. speakeroldname: Mr. A. C. Cadieu (Meadow Lake) moved:
subtopic: FRENCHMAN BUTTE-HEINSBURG-RAILWAY FACILITIES-SUGGESTED REFERENCE OF QUESTION TO COMMITTEE
speechtext:
That the question of providing railway facilities and services between Frenchman Butte, Saskatchewan, and Heinsburg, Alberta, be referred to the standing committee on transport and communications, and that it be an instruction to the committee to inquire into, report upon and make recommendations with respect to the question within thirty days after it has been referred.
He said: Mr. Speaker, in proposing this motion I do so in the belief that the matter is one of considerable urgency and great importance not only to a large number of producing Canadians in northwestern Saskatchewan and northeastern Alberta but to the national economy as well. This is not the first occasion on which I have tried to impress upon the house the importance of this question. I would refer Your Honour to my remarks, reported in Hansard for January 13, 1967, page 11761, during the clause by clause consideration of the bill dealing with railway line abandonment.
At the present time there is no direct rail connection between Alberta and Saskatchewan north of the North Saskatchewan river. This leaves a huge gap in railway transportation in an area of Canada that is producing great benefits for the nation as a whole and whose potential in mineral development, mixed farming and other industry is tremendous.
Briefly the picture is that one east-west line of the C.P.R. ends at Meadow Lake, Saskatchewan, leaving a gap of approximately 75 miles between that point and Grand Centre in Alberta. A little farther south a C.N.R. line ends at St. Walburg, leaving a transportation gap of about 50 miles between there and Heinsburg, Alberta. Farther south still, and
January 29, 1968	COMMONS
just north of the Saskatchewan river, a C.N.R. branch line stops at Frenchman Butte. This line branches off the St. Walburg line of the C.N.R. at Spruce Lake and is 28 miles in length. Between Frenchman Butte and Heins-burg, Alberta, is a gap of 38 miles. This pyramid of missing railway connections leaves no rail transportation north of the North Saskatchewan river from Edmonton to North Battleford and Prince Albert. I do not believe that there can be any sound, progressive development of the rich mineral and agricultural areas of northwestern Saskatchewan and northeastern Alberta until this gap is filled.
I suggest that the soundest method of filling the gap is by the C.N.R. completing the 38 mile stretch between Frenchman Butte and Heinsburg. Unfortunately, Mr. Speaker, the branch line between Spruce Lake and Frenchman Butte is one of those slated to go under the axe of rail line abandonment. That is why I believe the matter is urgent, as I said earlier, not only for the people of the area but for the whole country. Because it is urgent and important I believe it advisable for this question to be placed before the standing committee on transport and communications immediately, with instructions to the committee to make recommendations upon it within 30 days. I ask the house to consider my motion favourably from the standpoint of the national interest. I ask hon. members to send this question to the committee before it is too late to do anything about it.
I remember the time 40 years ago when the railways were fighting to get rights to build westward through our area. I remember the great plans and announcements of the railway at the time the first sod was turned at Shell-brook in 1928 for the line which the railway company today dismisses as a mere branch line and expendable. In those days the veteran settlers and pioneers of the area were promised that it was to be the start of a great main line connection linking Prince Albert, North Battleford and other cities and towns in Saskatchewan with their western neighbours north of the river. For half a century this dream has been dangled before our eyes. Now after 50 years of empty promises we are to lose even the dream through the proposed plan of rail line abandonment. I urge hon. members to consider this matter carefully before it is too late.
The C.N.R. even went so far some years ago as to prepare a right of way, a roadbed
DEBATES	6097
Extension of Railway Facilities for the connection between St. Walburg and Grand Centre. But this too was abandoned. Today trees grow on that roadbed. That link is dead.
But the shorter and easier route a little to the south remains a sound possibility. It is comparatively easy ground from a construction point of view. It takes in the old district of Fort Pitt, Onion Lake and Seekaskootch Indian reserve which is excellent mixed farming territory. A railway line would help greatly to open up an area fabulously rich in mineral wealth.
I recall how many people scoffed when the former Conservative government undertook to encourage the construction of the Pine Point railway line. It was laughed at as a wilderness line, a line to nowhere. We all know today the manner in which this project paid off for Canada. I believe that the line I am suggesting be considered will also pay big dividends for the people of the area and, through them, for Canada as a whole. Apart entirely from consideration of dividends and other payments I believe this line is required in the name of simple justice. It would be the fulfilment of promises and undertakings made years ago by both railway companies when they were desperate to acquire rights to build lines in that area. For years they reaped the advantage of a selective system of railroad operation that had nothing to do with the convenience or commercial interests of the residents but rested solely on profits for the railroads.

The railway has an obligation to the people of this area to construct this one small line. If the railway is unwilling to do so voluntarily it should be compelled by parliament to do it. I believe I have said sufficient to convince reasonable people that this question deserves immediate consideration by the standing committee. It has been brought forward by myself on numerous occasions. I have been joined in my representations by the hon. member for Athabasca (Mr. Bigg) and the hon. member for Vegreville (Mr. Fane) who has seconded this motion as being the best means by which to insist upon early consideration of this matter.
In concluding my remarks I should like to say that this question is one which is of truly urgent as well as national and local importance. I trust that the house will see fit to refer the matter to the standing committee on transport and communications in the terms outlined in my notice of motion.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, may I first answer the hon. gentleman's question concerning the produce and the wealth lying along this line which would warrant such an expenditure. This is very good mixed farming country. In linking up with Heins-burg, Alberta there would be access to what I believe is one of the wealthiest salt mines in northern Canada. All the way through there are mineral deposits. This line would link up with the Indian reservation at Seekaskootch. This is a large tract of good farm land. In fairness to these people I think this railway line is warranted. It would give them access to Prince Albert for their timber and pulp-wood. This Paradise Hill country is considered to be one of the best farming areas in northwestern Saskatchewan. From Frenchman Butte the terrain over the 38 miles is all good mixed farming country.
I cannot understand why this link was not constructed in the first place. I do not know how the railway expected the line to be a paying proposition when 38 miles were left unfinished. It is for these reasons that I have brought up this matter many times before the committee on transport and communications. I have also brought it up with Mr. Gordon. He agreed with me. I asked him how in the world they could have expected this line to be a paying proposition. When one looks at the map and notices the geographical location of this line one will see that the north Saskatchewan river is a natural barrier to the south and that there is no connecting railway line. All three attempts to have a railway line constructed across that provincial boundary have failed. We cannot understand the reason for this.
I could point out at great length the reasons that this line should be built. For instance, the rail line to Fort McMurray was built to serve all the people of northern Canada, yet in Saskatchewan we have no way to get to it without going around through Edmonton. These are injustices which the people have

put up with for half a century. I hope this answers the hon. member's question.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to thank the hon. member for Meadow Lake (Mr. Cadieu) for his answer. I asked the question because the last time a bill in respect of the C.N.R. was put through the house it concerned a new line which involved an extension in the Kenora region of my constituency of Kenora-Rainy River. Before speaking at this time, I went through the debates and I discerned three conditions which must be met before the government would undertake to promote such a bill in the House of Commons.
The first provision was that the line should be capable of doing three things. First, it should provide a substantial increase in the revenue of the railway. More important, this was described in terms of a substantial profit. In this particular case, which is described in Hansard for April 25, 1966, page 4267, the profit was outlined as $1 million per year. Second, the line must have a specific purpose. In other words, there would have to be some form of development that was available to it before the government would undertake to raise the money for the railway line. In this case it was the development of a new open pit mine known as the Griffith mine, owned and controlled by the Steel Company of Canada, which would be producing one and a half million tons of iron pellets annually.
The third item was that there must be a guarantee of traffic. In other words, the mine must contract with the railway to provide the railway with a stated amount of tonnage per year in order to provide for the proper paying off of the cost of building the line. In that case the railway went so far as to demand that in the event the production of pellets did not come up to the anticipated levels the mine would pay the difference in revenue to the railway company. So the railway was properly protected and was guaranteed the profit and revenue necessary to operate the line. This seems to be the procedure that has been followed in other cases.
Canadian National Railways is working on another line at present, the 235-mile Alberta resources railway which it is building under a leasing agreement with the province of Alberta. I gather this is the line to which the hon. member referred when he mentioned Fort McMurray.

If anyone looks at our patchwork transportation lines he will see that this historian, Mr. Lower, I believe, was not very far off the mark.

There are one or two remarks which I should like to make. I think the hon. member and the people whom he represents have become apprehensive about the situation which might develop because the line running west of St. Walburg is not protected by the order protecting certain lines throughout western Canada until 1975. I can fully understand their apprehension because it appears to me there will be some farmers in the area who will be 20 miles farther away from an elevator and from a market for their grain, if indeed the C.N.R. come to the Canadian Transport Commission and is successful in an application to abandon that line. I am sure the application for the abandonment of that portion of the railway line has already been made because I think applications have been made for all unprotected lines. But of course hon. members know that what is holding this up at the present time, and quite properly so, is the need for establishing a costing formula to determine how much revenue and how much cost can properly be attributed to any of these branch lines. I think it is only proper to hold up the abandonment of these unprotected lines until such time as members of the house and other interested parties across the country are able to agree on the factors that will go into the costing formula.
I will not take time today to explain this matter, but let me say that in my experience the figures advanced by the railway companies are quite often loaded in favour of their argument. In light of the fact that at present we do not have an accepted formula, I can understand the additional apprehension which exists. I do not know whether or not the farmers near Heinsburg in Alberta pay a higher rate for the transportation of their grain through Edmonton and then to the
January 29, 1968	COMMONS
lakes, or whether this is calculated as if there were a line going across. This is something else the committee should look into. For example, do these farmers pay more per hundredweight or per bushel than farmers closer to Edmonton, taking into consideration the fact there is a backhaul to the west and then a haul to the east again? If they do, and if that is unjustified, then of course I believe these farmers have the right to press, as they have been doing through the hon. member and his colleague the hon. member for Athabasca (Mr. Bigg), to have this line built, or an adjustment made in the freight rate which would take into account the capital cost of construction. There is always of course the matter of the volume of traffic today and the potential traffic that would be moving east from the area in the immediate future. This traffic might include such things as the rather extensive production of salt from two or three mines in the area, as well as the present and potential grain production for export from the area.
[DOT] (6:50 p.m.)
I suppose the decision is one for the management of the Canadian National, based to some extent on these considerations. I feel it is important also that the members of this house who represent the people in the area, as well as many people in other parts of the prairies, ought to have a thorough explanation from someone as to why it is uneconomic to construct this line. The hon. member for Meadow Lake (Mr. Cadieu) said he could not understand why this gap had been left in the first place. He could not understand why, over the last half century, no action had been taken to fill the gap. I am sure he has kept himself well informed of all the developments and the explanations that have been given by the railway company throughout these years. If he is still able to say he cannot understand why action has not been taken long since, then I believe the members of this house, through the committee on transport and communications, have an obligation to find those answers for him.
I do not know what it would cost to build that railway today. The hon. member for Vegreville (Mr. Fane) suggested that in 1927 the cost would have been a little over $3 million. I am sure the cost today would be two or three times that. This would be one of the factors which would have to be related to the amount of revenue and the volume of traffic that would result from the construction of the line.

Extension of Railway Facilities
However, Mr. Speaker, this is not the only serious problem existing in connection with gaps in railway lines on the prairies. In my constituency there is an unprotected line from Hays to Suffield. If this line, about 30 miles in length were removed, a similar situation would be created to the one about which the hon. member has been complaining. This railway line, however, is in existence, as is the bridge over the South Saskatchewan river. I know that the figures advanced by the Canadian Pacific Railway respecting the number of carloadings originating on sidings along that line were not substantiated by the figures available through the Board of Transport Commissioners. Here, again, we need to have these facts substained before the committee. As I said earlier, we have been able to investigate and ascertain that the railways were advancing figures that were not accurate. Perhaps they have been doing the same thing in the case about which the hon. members complained affecting northeastern Alberta and northeastern Saskatchewan. I believe we should have available to give evidence before the committee, those experts who have studied the matter. Then we could give consideration to whether or not the capital required is reasonable in relation to the potential earnings.
Another point mentioned by the hon. member which impressed me was that it is not always a matter of dollars and cents so far as the railway is concerned. There is also the matter of providing an equal opportunity for the people throughout western Canada to operate their farms and have facilities available which would enable them to be competitive with other parts of the prairies. Even if there were a slight loss, therefore, I would favour the construction of this line. If a substantial loss were projected by the officials of the railway company appearing before the committee, then of course we would have to decide how great a loss would be justified in order to satisfy the requirements of the people in that area.
I know the hon. member for Nickel Belt (Mr. Fawcett) said this was a rich farming area today and probably will continue to be. Indeed there is probably a lot more land up there that could be exploited for farm purposes. This would add to the potential volume of traffic. So, Mr. Speaker, I am going to close my remarks at this time. Good arguments have been advanced for the committee to hear this case. I would hope a situation like this could be corrected, provided the evidence

speechtext:
It being seven o'clock I do now leave the chair.
At seven o'clock the committee took recess.

AFTER RECESS

The committee resumed at 8 p.m.

Mr. Chairman, before supper I was making a few remarks relative to the amendment now before the committee wherein I was expressing my surprise at the reasoning put forward by the minister. If the committee would bear with me I will repeat the essence of my remarks, which simply is this.
We have gone to the trouble of enshrining in clause 2 (c) of the bill the right to freedom of expression, subject to the applicable statutes and regulations. Bearing in mind that

DEBATES	January 29, 1968
there is considerable concern in the country about the right to receive programs that are broadcast and that there is an immense disparity in the reception of programs in different parts of the country, in view of the many new opportunities now afforded our citizens, through the means of cablevision and other systems, to receive all programs that are available, I thought it essential to include in the bill a right that goes hand in hand with freedom of expression, namely freedom to see and hear all broadcast programs that are available.
My present amendment before the committee has been watered down from the original version I first proposed last Tuesday night, in that it seeks to give Canadians the right to receive all programs. The minister has suggested that this would open the door to unlimited demands that all programs be made available. With respect, Mr. Chairman, I do not follow that interpretation of my amendment. If it were included in this paragraph of clause 2 it would in any event be subject to the relevant statutes and regulations. Under the terms of the bill the cablevision systems, rebroadcast systems-rediffusion systems, as they are called-are brought within the control of the regulatory body.
I do not think it can be suggested that the inclusion of the freedom to receive all programs could be given any wider or narrower application than freedom of expression, because both rights are subject to the relevant statutes and regulations. Therefore, to be consistent, if the minister suggests that the inclusion of the words "freedom to receive all programs" would open the door to all sorts of demands for rebroadcasting, amplifying or rediffusing all kinds of signals without regard to the law, then she must also say that the same construction can be placed on the words "freedom of expression", about which she should have the same fears.
There can be but one reason, Mr. Chairman, for the refusal of the minister to include in the bill an affirmation of the right of the people to receive all broadcasts, namely that the government is insisting on the right of censorship so it can refuse citizens of this country reception of certain programs.
This amendment is not placing upon the government the burden of making sure that everyone in Canada should have the right to receive all programs wherever they may originate. That seemed to be the purport of the minister's comments. My amendment cannot be read in that way. All I am contending
January 29. 1968

is that if the amendment is accepted, and this expression included in the bill, it would affirm that there is a right to receive all programs. I does not add one iota to the duty of the government or any regulatory body to ensure that those programs are made available; neither does it detract from their authority to establish the necessary rules and regulations governing the broadcasting or distribution of such programs.
Therefore, Mr. Chairman, unless the minister can show that my reasoning is unsound and that there is a difference in principle between the right to receive and freedom of expression, the government should accept this amendment. It should give equal weight to the other freedom that I suggest is a corollary of the freedom of expression, namely the right to hear and see all programs.

Mr. Chairman, I have listened to the remarks of the hon. member for Ed-monton-Strathcona with a great deal of interest. I also heard some of the debate last week. When the hon. member originally proposed his amendment the minister was not too happy with its wording and thought that the week end might produce a more satisfactory amendment. The minister has kindly given a further reply today which seemed to deal with some of the semantics involved here, as well as some of the difficulties created by granting an unlimited right to reception of programs.
I think the remarks of the hon. member for Edmonton-Strathcona demand very close scrutiny by the committee, because in this bill we are talking about freedom of speech or freedom of expression. Hon. members opposite are Liberals in the true sense-certainly they are in the classical sense-and they should be most concerned about this clause in the bill. Those to my left who have talked so eloquently about freedom of speech and ensuring that clause 2 (d) does not prescribe any sort of censorship or direction should, I suggest, pay very close attention to this particular paragraph.
If the present wording of the clause were accepted by the committee we would be admitting not only that the licence to broadcast should be controlled but that the right to freedom of speech is ensured. Yet, in remote areas, the freedom of Canadians to hear or see programs carried by cable is severely restricted. That freedom is governed by this bill, since what is involved is not broadcasting but reception only.
Canadian Policy on Broadcasting [DOT] (8:10 p.m.)
Regardless of the generality of the principle of the freedom to hear and see via cable television, another criticism must be levelled at this clause. This bill is another one of those that try to define some sort of national policy and to bring together various regions of the country. I am thinking particularly of the Atlantic area. That area is not one of the great growth areas of Canada, it is not Ontario or Quebec and does not have all the competitive companies that are now engaged in the cable television field. It is not proposed to put many television stations into that area to cover it. I think one new station is to be installed by the C.E.C., and another by C.T.V. An application is under way with respect to a station at Moncton, but that station will extend an existing network. I do not think it will be an originating station.
In an area that has not much growth you do not find that operators will open lucrative television stations; nor will you find many originating stations in that area. This afternoon the minister talked about the necessity to have originating stations. Certainly I should like to know what she and her officials foresee will be the future of originating stations in the Atlantic area. Where you have no originating stations, or few of them, and where the country is slow growing, the only way that many Canadians in that part of the country can receive programs is through the medium of cable television. This bill will restrict the development of cable television, and bring it under the broadcasting legislation. I have been informed, nevertheless, that it is extremely difficult to get anyone in the department even to listen to a request from the east for cable television.
What good is it to have freedom of speech, which as Canadians we all ought to have, if we cannot see and hear programs that are carried by television or by cable television? This is almost the reverse side of the coin; it is almost a reverse type of censorship to which the hon. member for Edmonton-Strathcona referred previously.
Members of the committee have often talked about freedom of speech. To a certain extent we may have abused that freedom here. When we talk about the freedom of speech we cannot divorce it from the freedom to hear-the right to hear and see all programs that are to be heard and seen. You cannot take away that right from those who live in parts of the country that do not have a good growth rate and that do not provide
6106	COMMONS
Canadian Policy on Broadcasting lucrative markets for originating stations, such as you have in Ontario and Quebec. I hope hon. members of the committee will find favour with and support the amendment moved by the hon. member for Edmonton-Strathcona.
Surely, Mr. Chairman, in such an important matter it is only a question of evolving the right phrase to fit the circumstances. Surely the law officers, the minister and her officials could find a way of bringing some protection in, under this clause. I think they should try to follow the reasoning of the hon. member for Edmonton-Strathcona in the language they use.
We talk about freedom of speech, and yet, when it comes to the potential development of cable television for the Atlantic provinces, the freedom to see and hear is to be denied to some of the people of the areas. We ought to pay some attention to the freedom to see and to hear.
