speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, as the last speaker, the hon. member for Digby-Annapo-lis-Kings has stated, clause 2(c) is the heart of the matter, particularly when you consider that the right of free speech is being trampled underfoot by those who favour the adoption of such a clause as 2(c).
I was speaking the other night on this clause when my time expired. At that time I referred to a judgment of the Supreme Court of British Columbia, to which the Secretary of State herself had referred me. As I said, I have discussed it more than once with her. I wanted to advise the committee of the contents of that judgment because they are very, very vital to the question under discussion right now.
I pointed out that the province of British Columbia had endeavoured to gain control over the reception of radio signals, or television signals because, after gaining control over the reception operation, they would be able to regulate and tax such installations. The cablevision companies in Victoria and the lower mainland of British Columbia took the case to the British Columbia Supreme Court, asking for a ruling on the matter and maintaining that they were under federal jurisdiction. But, in giving the judgments that they did on the matter, the Supreme Court of British Columbia made reference to decisions of the Privy Council of Great Britain. These

DEBATES	January 29, 1968
decisions clearly establish that in the broadcasting world you cannot divide the transmitter from the receiver.
I should like to refer to some pages that I have before me. Bear in mind that the Secretary of State herself asked me to read the judgment, although I had read it several times before she referred me to it. I got an extra copy of it from the Supreme Court of Canada library.
I have here in my hand the judgment of the Supreme Court of British Columbia, as recorded in the Dominion Law Reports. The case is in re Public Utilities Commission and Victoria Cablevision Limited, et al. The learned judges of the Supreme Court of British Columbia said in part:
The receiving of the programs by air is beyond doubt within the exclusive jurisdiction of the Dominion. In He Regulation & Control of Radio Communication, A.-G. Que. v. A.-G. Can., (1932)
2 D.L.R. 81 (1932) A.C. 304, 39 C.R.C. 49, (1932)
1 W.W.R. 563,-
That is clear to the Secretary of State. She is a lawyer.
-Viscount Dunedin in delivering the judgment of the Privy Council stated at p. 85:
"Now does broadcasting fall within the excepted matters? Their Lordships are of opinion that it does, falling in (a) within both the words "telegraphs" and the general words "undertakings connecting the province with any other or others of the provinces or extending beyond the limits of the province"."
And at p. 86:
"Once it is conceded, as it must be, keeping in view the duties under the Convention, that the transmitting instrument must be so to speak under the control of the dominion, it follows in their Lordships' opinion that the receiving instrument must share its fate. Broadcasting as a system cannot exist without both a transmitter and a receiver. The receiver is indeed useless without a transmitter and can be reduced to a nonentity if the transmitter closes. The system cannot be divided into two parts, each independent of the other."
The receiver is indeed useless without a transmitter and can be reduced to a nonentity if the transmitter closes. The system cannot be divided into two parts, each independent of the other.
[DOT] (8:20 p.m.)
I have a second opinion to read to you also, Mr. Chairman, but this bears exactly on the point under discussion in clause 2(c) where the Canadian cabinet is endeavouring to split the right of free speech in two by making great mouth filling statements and high sounding platitudes about the fact that the right to freedom of expression is unquestioned. What good is the freedom of expression if people are not allowed to hear what is being said? Of all the idle, empty phrases I have seen in my life I have never seen the equal of this, that
January 29, 1968

the Department of Transport specifies only properly licensed stations.
What is this hogwash about saying that the C.A.T.V. signals must come from properly licensed stations? No C.A.T.V. station in Canada has ever asked for the right to pick up any other signal than that of a properly licensed station. Why make this foufaraw on this matter? It reminds me of the story of the divinity student who was relating his experiences in preaching on the subject of defective speaking. The student pointed out that sometimes he was not too sure of his statements. Ke said, "I am not too convinced in my own mind that what I am telling the congregation is correct doctrine. Sometimes I hesitate to speak, and lower my voice". But his professor said, to him "When you are on weak ground shout and stamp your feet; the weaker your argument, the louder you shout and the harder you stamp your feet."
Louder, louder.

Why are we bringing in this argument about a properly licensed station? The C.A.T.V. never picks up anything else. Then they bring in the business about pirate stations. No C.A.T.V. station ever picks up a pirate station. In commenting on the minister's remarks about pirate stations, I should like to point out that she makes a backhanded reference to not wanting people to listen to unlicensed stations. If there were unlicensed stations on the Atlantic or Pacific coasts I am sure you would only need to tell the fine people of British Columbia or Nova Scotia that they should not listen to those stations, to build up the biggest audience a radio or television station ever had. I am sure the minister must have been reading about the wreck of a pirate ship in the maritimes in recent days. The minister states:
Technically it would be possible to set up a broadcast or a rebroadcast station and make its programs available to everyone. However, I do not think the B.B.G. should be required to license them simply because such stations are technically feasible.
Once again we are off on a tangent. We are talking about C.A.T.V. stations which are nothing but reception centres; there is no broadcasting involved. They make no use of the air waves. But, the minister says that technically it would be possible to set up a broadcast or a rebroadcast station, and she does not think the B.B.G. should be required to licence them simply because such stations are technically feasible. I could not agree more. I am
January 29, 1968

old enough to remember the four-month period back around 1930 when the people who were trying to get into the radio world were screaming that they should not be licensed, and that the Canadian government had no right to say that they could or could not go on the air. The only difficulty is that electronically there are only so many channels available for radio stations, and in order to prevent congestion on the air someone has to authorize certain stations to use certain channels. For a period of time the United States government, the Mexican government and the Canadian government agreed that they would not restrict applications for radio licences. There are certainly a few male members of this house-none of the women are old enough-who will recall the episode about 35 years ago when they allowed all those people who wanted to do so to go on the air, and you could not pick up a station and make intelligent use of it because of the interference from other stations, some with weak power and nearby, and others with strong power and a distance away.
Then they decided they must limit the number of people who could get into broadcasting. A certain number of the channels in the air were limited to Canada, a certain number were limited to Mexico and a fair number were limited to the United States. In the case of C.A.T.V. the number of channels on the air has nothing to do with their applications. They have no use of the airwaves; they simply pick up the program in the air and transmit it by wire to their subscribers. Again, in her speech of Friday afternoon, the minister said this:
Other considerations come into play, such as whether or not a C.A.T.V. or a rebroadcast station of some kind should be licensed in a given area.
What balderdash is involved here? Other considerations come into play, such as whether or not a C.A.T.V. or a rebroadcast station of some kind should be licensed in a given area. Well, what did they do in Wawa? There was already a radio station in there, and they put in a rebroadcasting station right on top of the station at Wawa.
What does the minister mean when she says that other considerations come into play, such as whether or not a C.A.T.V. or a rebroadcast station of some kind should be licensed? She is making out that they are incompatible one with the other. We have a concrete case in Wawa where the C.B.C. put in a rebroadcasting station on top of the
Canadian Policy on Broadcasting C.A.T.V. They do not interfere with each other. One is a broadcasting unit making use of the airwaves, and the C.A.T.V. is a reception centre. They are not incompatible. There is no need to make a statement like that except to confuse the issue. Then we were told by the minister on Friday:
Sometimes the B.B.G. turns down such applications because they believe that a broadcasting station will at some time in the future be built in the area and this would be more in the interests of the community concerned.
Who says that it will be in the interests of the community concerned. If the people in Napanee, Prescott and Gananoque wish to have a C.A.T.V. installation so that they can pick up more programs than are available to them over the Kingston station, or the one or two Ottawa stations which are available there, that is the concern of the people in the area, and nobody else. Why should people be denied the right of freedom of choice in picking up television programs from other stations that are available to them while they are waiting for another station to be put into their area? What would you think of a situation in which a community wants a highway built so that they could bring in trucks and motorcars-perhaps an area in northern Ontario or northern Saskatchewan-if the government said that they would not give them a highway because it is quite possible that a railway may go in there in the future? The people would not stand for such an answer.
Now, however, the Secretary of State and the cabinet are trying to tell the people in Napanee, Gananoque and Prescott that they cannot look at any stations other than the presently available stations because in the future the C.B.C. might wish to put in another station. Mind you, they say they are not stopping their plans, that they are really just pulling them in. But how long will it be before they put a second station in that area? In the meantime they deny these people freedom of viewing,
[DOT] (8:40 p.m.)
Then we have the Secretary of State saying this:
The difficulty that both justice and the B.B.G. inform me they see in this amendment is that the phrase it seeks to add to the bill means different things to different people.
There is an argument, I am telling you. We have not heard that more than a million times in the past. That is, we cannot do something because a phrase means different things to different people. What about the clause on national unity that we were discussing the
January 29, 1968

Canadian Policy on Broadcasting other day and again this afternoon, when the hon. member for Burnaby-Richmond pointed out that the phrase "national unity" is or could be an entirely different thing from the phrase "Canadian unity"? If you are going to argue about two nations in this country you are going to have national unity practised by two different peoples. The hon. member for Burnaby-Richmond was endeavouring to have the clause read "Canadian unity" so there could be solidification of the situation.
We were told by the minister on Friday that she does not like the amendment suggested by the hon. member for Edmonton-Strathcona because justice and the B.B.G., forsooth, advise her that they seek to add a phrase which means different things to different people. That is why we have judges, because one firm says the law says this and another firm says the law says that, so obviously it means different things to different people. We have judges to decide. I should like to see any phrase in the English language that has only one meaning. We are given this puerile excuse that the B.B.G. and justice have informed the Secretary of State that the phrase seeks to add something which means different things to different people. Every phrase means different things to different people.
I regret having to say this, but in Hansard of Friday afternoon at page 6039, and carrying over to the next page, the Secretary of State is recorded as having said this:
These signals may come from a C.A.T.V. station-
I have said before, and I must repeat again, that the minister does not know what she is talking about, because a C.A.T.V. system does not issue a signal. The minister stands in her place here and endeavours to persuade this House of Commons to vote in a certain manner by making a statement that is absolutely incorrect. This is the same thing as trying to tell you that water runs uphill or that black is white. You would not swallow that. The minister does not know what she is talking about when she says these signals may come from a C.A.T.V. station. C.A.T.V. stations do not issue signals; but the statement has been made, and there you are.
This is on all fours with a situation that developed in the committee on broadcasting, films and assistance to the arts. We had expert witnesses there and one morning we had the expert of experts. The minister knows who he is, but I cannot place him now. He made the flat footed suggestion to the committee in answer to a question by me that

in the United States C.A.T.V. stations are licensed up to 50 subscribers. I never heard such a thing and I said to this expert of experts, "What are you talking about; where is this licensing authority?" He replied "yes; yes there is such an authority up to 50 subscribers." I have never heard of a C.A.T.V. station that works with as few as 50 subscribers.
During our noon adjournment I telephoned two authorities I know in western Canada and two people in Washington and I found there is no licensing authority in the United States of America for C.A.T.V. stations. We came back in the afternoon to an in camera session of that broadcasting committee. I thought that the expert of experts who had made this false statement in the morning would be there in the afternoon. The in camera session carried right on and finished its work about half past three. At that point a gentleman came over to me, also from the Department of the Secretary of State and said to me: "I want to tell you, sir, that there is no licensing authority in the United States. That was a mistake made this morning." Well, I might state that in the parlance of the street I really chewed his head off.
At that time I said to him: "What in the name of heaven do you mean by telling me, after the committee has brought in its report and has met in camera, that information given to us this morning is false information? Why do you tell me after the committee has risen that it is false?" He said to me he was not the man who made the statement in the morning. I said: "Oh, yes, everybody in the civil service who is responsible is always away on something much more important."
Here we have the minister herself standing up and stating that these signals may come from a C.A.T.V. station. This is a false statement because it is impossible; but it is given to you in evidence in order to persuade you to take some course of action. I say to you that in the committee on broadcasting we were given false information which was corrected after the committee rose. If we are going to make decisions on that kind of information we should reconsider the bill very carefully, clause by clause and sentence by sentence.
Then again on Friday afternoon the minister said:
There is no quarrel with the proposition that operators who are licensed and lawfully transmitting signals should be able to broadcast to all.
January 29, 1968

We are not even talking about that, and no one is quarrelling with it. We are talking about the right of people to receive signals that have been properly and lawfully authorized. Why bring in this line of hokum? There is no quarrel with the proposition that operators who are licensed and lawfully transmitting signals should be able to broadcast to everyone; but those are broadcasters. This phrase, the right to freedom of expression-
I regret to interrupt the hon. gentleman but his allotted time has now expired. Is the committee ready for the question?

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I found the remarks made by the hon. member for York-Humber (Mr. Cowan) very interesting, and I think that if someone intervenes between his two speeches, he will perhaps be able to continue his observations.
That is why I think I should say that freedom of expression implies also, as the hon. member for York-Humber pointed out so ably, freedom for each individual to hear the programs he wants.

Canadian Policy on Broadcasting be permitted to look at because a second television station might be opened in the future? How ridiculous can the government's stand be on a matter of this nature?
The Secretary of State went on to say:
They cannot receive all these signals unless something brings them to their sets. The C.A.T.V. operator might reply by saying:	"I have six
stations I want to transmit. The regulations say I cannot. I must transmit all 12, because parliament says everyone has a right to receive everything that is available."
Parliament should say that everyone has the right to receive everything that is available. As I said before, I do not pick up four television programs at one time on my home set. They are all available to me, but I do not pick them up simultaneously. I pick them up individually whenever I may wish to do so. For the Secretary of State to use the argument to a C.A.T.V. operator that he must transmit all 12 signals because parliament says everyone has the right to receive everything that is available is childish in the extreme. Why should a Canadian be limited only to the local T.V. station when more channels are available to him through an installation such as C.A.T.V. which is legal and proper in every way and which we have licensed in many parts of Canada?
I have already referred to the fact that it is stated in the B.B.G. report for the year ended March 31, 1967 that the Department of Transport has made 91 informal references to them on applications for C.A.T.V. licences. In making these references to the B.B.G. they said that 84 of the 91 applications would not compete with the local broadcaster. I have already asked why the cabinet is so solicitous of the local broadcaster. Why does he require protection from competition of the daily newspapers which sell advertising in the area? The newspapers are not protected against the T.V. operator, yet the T.V. operator is to be protected by the government against any competition which might make his economic life a little hard. The report states that C.A.T.V. must not be licensed because it can hurt the economic life of the local T.V. station.
I have in my hand the annual reports of the B.B.G. for the year ending March 31, 1963/64, 1964/65 and 1965/66. I have placed on the order paper, and it will appear in Wednesday's issue, a request to the Secretary of State to advise us what applications have been turned down for C.A.T.V. licences in
these three years, because we are told the following in the report ended March 31, 1965:
In the fiscal year ended March 51, 1965, the board examined 59 such applications and found that 46 of them, in its judgment, would not make the operation of existing T.V. stations uneconomical or inhibit the provision of alternate service.
This means that in that year 13 applications were turned down. I have asked to be advised which 13 areas were denied the privilege of freedom of speech, the right to look at whatever stations they could bring on a C.A.T.V. application by a C.A.T.V. installation, and the reasons for those refusals.
As I pointed out, in the year ended March 31, 1967 seven applications were turned down, two of which were in Pembroke, and since then the B.B.G. has informally advised the Minister of Transport to grant a licence to a third applicant. Also, since March 31, 1967, the B.B.G. said, an application for a C.A.T.V. licence in Clermont, Quebec was turned down; but now that it is after April 1, All Fool's Day, they are in favour of granting a licence to Clermont, Quebec, and it has been granted. Why is it that the B.B.G. has reversed its decisions that were evidently made on proper grounds, as set forth in their learned opinions, as each application is received and dealt with?
In the year ended March 31, 1966, the
B.	B.G. stated that the minister referred 82
C.	A.T.V. applications to the board. The number included applications for new licences, extensions of existing systems, and changes in the channels carried. It stated further:
The board found that 72 of them, in its judgment, would not make the operation of existing T.V. stations uneconomical or inhibit the provision of alternative service.
In the year ended March 31, 1966, the board turned down 10 applications. In the year ended March 31, 1965 they turned down 13 applications, and in the year ended March 31, 1967 they turned down seven applications, making a total of 30. I think the public of Canada and parliament are entitled to know which 30 areas have been deprived of the privilege of C.A.T.V. installations. It would also be interesting to know what applications are being considered by the B.B.G. at present.
I regret the hon. member for Kamloops is not here because I showed him a letter which I received from a man who pointed out that in Vancouver they have seven channels from which they can select the one they want to see, but when he and his wife go to visit a daughter and son-in-law in Kamloops there is

January 29, 1968

only one program available to them, namely the local T.V. station in Kamloops. Yet applications have been made for a C.A.T.V. installation in Kamloops and they are in the hands of the Minister of Transport. I am advised by the hon. member for Kamloops that there is a freeze on until parliament deals with the Broadcasting Act now before us. Why should the people in Vancouver be given such freedom of choice when it comes to television programs while the people in Kamloops are told to look at one local station and nothing else? They are told what is good for them. The people in Vancouver can do what they like; there are too many of them to be browbeaten, but there is a small group in Kamloops which will be told what to look at.
The other evening the hon. member for Prince Edward-Lennox told us of another application which has been turned down from a Mr. Dawson who applied for a C.A.T.V. licence in Napanee. I happen to know of two other applications in the Kingston area which have been turned down. Why does the B.B.G. interfere with the right of the people to pick up the programs they might wish, over the C.A.T.V. installation, which will not cost the Canadian taxpayers a cent, for which subscribers to the C.A.T.V. service have to pay in monthly instalments, and for which they are willing to pay as is obvious from the tremendous number of subscribers which has built up over the years?
[DOT] (9:10 p.m.)
I should now like to revert to the comments made by the Secretary of State in explaining why she could not accept the proposed amendment of the hon. member for Edmon-ton-Strathcona. Let me refer again to the comments made by the minister on Friday. She said she was told by Justice and the Board of Broadcast Governors that the ramifications of the suggested amendment were too wide and she was advised not to accept the amendment. We now find ourselves in the beautiful position where, in 1962, we screamed because the administration headed by Right Hon. J. G. Diefenbaker would not produce an opinion from the Department of Justice on the question of import and export taxes and the rebates that were made on tariff collections. We were told then that the government never produces these confidential, highly secret and very learned opinions that are exchanged between the Department of Justice and other divisions of the federal cabinet. So we screamed to the high heavens that this was not right. We were told
Canadian Policy on Broadcasting that the cabinet was accepting the advice and that we, in the opposition, had to accept the opinion of the law officers of the crown, because the law officers of the crown never make a mistake.
We, in the opposition, and the Secretary of State was one of them, objected to this high handed action on the part of the cabinet in telling the elected representatives of the people that what they wanted to see was being withheld from their eyes. Now the Secretary of State, who five years ago shrilled and trilled with the rest of us against the high handed action of the Diefenbaker cabinet, stands in her place and says she is told that the ramifications of the amendment are too wide and she is advised not to accept it. In view of the fact that the Diefenbaker cabinet never did produce the opinion of the law officers of the crown in 1962-and I hope the hon. lady does not forget that we turned out the Diefenbaker government-I am not going to ask for the production of the document today. I do not want to see the lady get up and ape the Diefenbaker cabinet by stating, "We cannot produce an opinion that is so anxiously demanded." She might have demanded such an opinion in 1962, and she was right then. If I ask for a copy of the opinion in 1968, she will tell me I am wrong. I do not like that kind of thinking. If you are right in 1962, then you are right in 1968. You cannot be right in 1962 and wrong in 1968 on the same issue. I believe there are reasonable people in this house who will agree with me on that point.
The hon. member for Peace River speaking on Friday afternoon made a very interesting comment to the Secretary of State when he said, as reported on page 6041 of Hansard:
I have not intervened in this discussion so far, but I believe it would be a serious error of judgment if we were to leave the subject in the absence of an indication that there is no restriction on the right to receive programs.
This clause has to be amended. The right of freedom of speech is too important to the people of Canada for a so-called Liberal government to allow a provision that the broadcaster's right to express himself is unquestioned to become the law of the land. Someone has to stand up for the individual viewer who wants to receive the programs that are being broadcast. There is no virtue in allowing people to broadcast programs and refusing the people of the nation the right to pick up those programs if they so desire. I ask the committee to support the amendment moved
6116	COMMONS
Canadian Policy on Broadcasting by the hon. member for Edmonton-Strath-cona. We dare not deny the right of freedom of speech to the people of this country unless we are going to admit we no longer have a democratic form of government.

As I indicated earlier to the minister, if the amendment was still too sweeping I would have another to suggest. The argument used by the minister against the amendment the other day was to the effect that the words "by any means whatever" made it too wide. This amendment has just been defeated. The minister's entire argument was based on the fact that the amendment referred to "all programs available". The reasoning of the minister and her advisers apparently was based on the premise that the right to receive was going to complicate the situation to such an extent that the obligation of the government to make programs available would be involved. Since this was the case, I felt that we should then move an amendment which would preserve the right or freedom to receive without running into the dangers the minister envisaged. I will just have to take it for granted that the hon. members who voted against the amendment listened to the minister's reasons and therefore rejected the amendment on that ground.
I shall therefore present to the committee an amendment which is free of that criticism and which I hope the minister and her supporters will be able to accept. The amendment I propose reads as follows:
Clause 2. subclause (c) of Bill C-163 is amended by inserting between the words "expression" and "subject" in line 19 thereof the following: "and the right of persons to receive programs".
The clause as amended would then read:
(c) all persons licensed to carry on broadcasting undertakings have a responsibility for the programs they broadcast but the right to freedom of expression and the right of persons to receive programs, subject only to generally applicable statutes and regulations, is unquestioned.
Now, Mr. Chairman, the argument in support of the right to receive programs is simply the argument in support of the freedom of speech. It is just useless to enshrine within an act such as the Broadcasting Act that there is a right to freedom of expression

DEBATES	January 29, 1968
unless, along with that, is the simple right to see and to hear what has been expressed. The amendment I have moved simply provides for the right to receive what has been broadcast or what has been expressed. This right is not a blanket right but is subject to the rules and regulations. I must confess that I am very surprised at the attitude shown by the minister's advisers in this regard, s (9:20 p.m.)
It is argued that there is a great difference today between the programs available in different parts of the country. Cablevision is available to some citizens and not others. We have yet to feel the benefit of satellite television which the government will have to regulate with a great deal of flexibility. We have not yet begun to handle problems created by educational television on high frequency channels.
The minister has expressed the present feeling of her advisers, which seems to be that because we have dared express the view in the amendment that Canadians should be given the right to freedom of reception, it must be rejected on the ground that it would open the door to additional difficulties. If this is the case, then I feel that her advisers will be unable to make the changes that are required in our programming patterns and our broadcasting patterns to meet availability of reception through the different media in operation.
Surely I am not unjustified in suggesting that some areas of Canada receive more programs than others. For example, Edmonton, Saskatoon and Regina have one or perhaps two channels and no cablevision. In Vancouver and Toronto a multiplicity of channels is available and the government seems disposed to continue this situation.
Surely it is only fair to suggest that the reason one group of Canadians has a choice of programs and another does not is because the government wants to keep its thumb on those who cannot escape government supervision. In a nutshell, the government is saying that although it cannot restrict reception of those Canadians who are close enough to the border to receive programs from the United States, it can restrict reception of those who subscribe to cablevision because it has the power to license such systems.
I am wondering, Mr. Chairman, why the minister will not accept this amendment. Does she want to control reception of programs because, in order to justify government expenditure on broadcasting, there must
January 29, 1968

be a guaranteed audience? Is it because these programs are not up to standard and that this captive audience would not watch them if other programs were made available? If the minister is not going to accept this amendment I trust she will advance further reasons for our not having satisfied the sensibilities of her advisers in this regard.
The reason I have moved this amendment to this particular paragraph of the clause and not to another clause, as suggested by the minister, is because this paragraph deals with the freedom of expression. A corollary of freedom of expression, I submit, is the freedom to see and hear programs. Therefore the amendment properly belongs to this paragraph.
Second, we must not forget that freedom of expression is limited by the responsibility of the government to make regulations which ensure that our airwaves are properly and regularly used. My amendment similarly would be subject to the relevant statutes and regulations.
I acknowledge the considerable interest of the members of the New Democratic party in this matter, their having voted with the minister on the last amendment. I hope this was because they were persuaded by the arguments of the minister that the amendment would create such demand for television channels, for cablevision, and so on, that the power to regulate in proper manner would be inhibited.
However, Mr. Chairman, even those who have such faith in regulation cannot find any such objection to the present amendment, which merely asks for freedom to receive programs along with the freedom of expression. I have not suggested reception of all programs broadcast "by any means whatsoever". There can be no implication here of Pressuring the government to meet any further demand. Neither would my amendment further inhibit the regulatory authority in any way.
Any suggestion that Canadians should be deprived of freedom to receive programs on the ground that some civil servant advisers are afraid of this right, or that it would cause more trouble in drafting regulations is, I submit, unacceptable. If that is their attitude, what is to prevent them from taking the next logical step? Having considered an application for a licence the authorities could tell the applicant that, although his application may not infringe the regulations, at some time in 27053-386J
Canadian Policy on Broadcasting the future they might want to draw up further regulations which might be jeopardized were the application granted. Surely if the government believes in freedom of speech the minister has the duty to see that somebody takes a stand somewhere.
All my amendment does is to continue the concept of freedom of speech by adding the freedom to receive what is expressed. There is nothing in my amendment to create difficulty and I trust the minister will accept it in the interest of free speech in this country.
[DOT] (9:30 p.m.)

Mr. Chairman, before you put the amendment may I say that I do not think my hon. friend really intended to make an attack on the civil service. Our civil servants are paid to give expert advice to members of the house who, obviously, are not experts themselves. They have the responsibility to advise those in the executive branch of the house how to do what the government has decided to do. I know the hon. member is very generous and does not mean to impute some improper motive to civil servants who are doing their proper job.
I am sorry that the hon. member talked to such length but it seemed, since he was entering such high flights of rhetoric, that it would be a pity to interrupt him to say that I was prepared to accept his amendment.
To say what?
The amendment is accepted?
Does the Secretary of State say she is prepared to accept the amendment?
That's what she said.

Mr. Chairman, referring to clause 2(i) that is before us now and which reads:
___facilities should be provided within the Canadian broadcasting system for educational broadcasting;
I can only ask this: Is there never going to be a halt at all on the amount of money that is to be spent in the broadcasting world, or do we simply keep on going and going, throwing money into the hopper for radio and television year after year, in ever increasing amounts?
Education, as we know and admit, is a provincial matter. While I regret that that is so-
Hear, hear.

-I have to admit it and live with it. But when we talk about spending money for increasing the facilities for education broadcasts, I mean it when I say that we are talking about the past and not about the future.
I cannot see spending money on educational broadcasting, on educational programs, and for a very self-evident reason. All the classes in certain grades are following a curriculum that is laid down generally by the provincial department of education. The end result is that the teachers in the various classes throughout the large and small municipalities will bring some children to the same examination point, let us say, in the month of June, so that they will all be equally taught to answer the questions that are put to them in the final examinations. But surely no one in

this house is going to say that all the children, day by day and week by week throughout the school year, are making the same progress and are discussing the same chapters in the prescribed books? We know for a fact that an epidemic may close a certain school for a week or so, and throw its students behind the other students in the same municipality and in the same grades.
I have always got a kick out of two girls who went to college and took the course in religious knowledge. I was a Presbyterian and enrolled in a Methodist institution. At least, it was Methodist when I was enrolled-Victoria University. They had a course in religious knowledge. Since there is nothing in religious knowledge that a Methodist can teach a Presbyterian, I never took it. But I did know of two girls who were taking religious knowledge and they had different professors, because of the schedule that had been handed to them.
One day one girl, walking across Queen's Park, said to the other, "How are you doing in religious knowledge?" The other girl replied, "We're doing very well. We're in the midst of original sin." The other girl said to her, "That's nothing, in the class I'm in we're past redemption."
I only tell you the story to show you that if two classes-
Whom are you speaking about?
I am speaking of two girls, my friend.
In original sin and past redemption?
I will admit I am in original sin where I am standing.
Oh, oh.

I gave you that little story to show that classes do not maintain the same speed. There are other reasons for that. Teachers vary in their ability to impart knowledge, and classes vary in their ability to receive the knowledge and to absorb it properly.
I have the great good fortune of having resided in Toronto for the past 50 years, and during the last several years in my work with the Toronto Star-

Good fortune or
misfortune?
January 29, 1968

-I had the opportunity of providing the school systems of Etobicoke, North York and Scarborough in particular, and some of the schools in the city of Toronto, with educational film. The use of educational film in the school systems of Canada is growing by leaps and bounds. The hon. member for Scarborough is an ex chairman of the board of education for the borough of North York.
Hear, hear.

I have to tell you that the educational film programs of the borough of North York, the borough of Scarborough and the borough of Etobicoke are without peer in the Dominion of Canada, and in my opinion they are certainly in the forefront of educational film in North America.
Each film is available to a classroom teacher. A great many of the films come from the National Film Board. They are not made available free of charge to the school boards, and in many, many cases the school boards accept contributions of educational film from firms that are willing to provide this assistance to the educational film division of the borough.
The interesting thing to me is that the Toronto Star used to supply-and it may to this day, for all I know-used to supply a couple of thousand feet of educational film every month to the educational film division of Scarborough, North York and Etobicoke.
The point I want to impress on members of the committee is this. The teachers used to tell each other that they valued the film highly. It was placed in the library of the local borough governing the school system, and when the teachers wanted it they simply requisitioned the film, or sent for it. It was run off over the school projector and the teacher instructed the class in the meaning of the pictures and the idea behind the entire film.
[DOT] (9:40 p.m.)
The fact that these films are placed in a central library and sent out to the individual schools as requested, shows that the individual classes are not studying the same subject at the same time throughout the school year. Are we going to be asked to invest millions of dollars in an educational broadcasting system that may very well prove unworkable? What hope is there of maintaining every grade 7 class in Ontario at the same speed of comprehension on the part of the children, and at
Canadian Policy on Broadcasting the same speed of instruction on the part of the teachers, throughout the year?
Individual classrooms can receive a benefit from educational film made available to them as their individual teachers request, but they will not receive the same advantage from educational film being shown to them over the airwaves of the nation. I believe this fact is self-evident.
The Secretary of State can state that clause 2 is only declaratory. I have been trying to tell the hon. member for Lotbiniere and the hon. member for Lapointe that I do not mind voting for a declaratory clause which deals with English and French because that declaratory clause does not say that we are going to spend now the money involved. But why should we have a declaratory statement that facilities should be provided for educational television within the Canadian broadcasting system? By having this clause we are making a half promise that we will spend millions of dollars in the future. I say that we do not need to make such a declaration. We do not need to make a commitment at the present time.
Educational matters are being adequately and very completely covered by the national film board series of films, and by the educational films available through provincial departments of education and through tourist bureaus. British Columbia will send into Ontario beautiful films which show the geographic and commercial features of British Columbia and British Columbia schools can get similar films from the province of Ontario and the province of Quebec. The beauty of this arrangement is that teachers are able to use those films in keeping with the progress of their classes.
If you bring in educational television on the national broadcasting system it is going to be like the bed of Procrustes. Every teacher is going to know, no matter whether his class is ready to receive it or not, that the eleventh lecture on the history of Canada will be shown on next Thursday morning. In an individual class lectures Nos. 8, 9 and 10 may have been delayed. Why should a child who has only had lectures Nos. 1 to 7 suddenly be exposed to lecture No. 11 simply because a national television education system says that will be the lecture to be shown at eleven o'clock the following Thursday morning?
I am speaking from knowledge of the system in the borough of York North, the borough of Scarborough and the borough of
January 29. 1968

Canadian Policy on Broadcasting Etobicoke which are in the forefront of matters pertaining to educational film. Teachers of classes in those boroughs can use educational films when they want to, and not when some broadcaster on the air feels impelled to lecture the children of a certain geographical division on a certain topic. I say this clause is unnecessary and should not be in a declaratory part of the bill, where it has no teeth.

Mr. Chairman, clause 2(i) reads as follows:
.-facilities should be provided within the Canadian broadcasting system for educational broadcasting;
Now, through a bill on broadcasting, the federal government is interfering in a field which, in accordance with the British North America Act, comes exclusively under the provincial jurisdiction. We know that the educational field comes under the provinces. I will be told that it deals with the equipment of educational broadcasting.
Mr. Chairman, for a hundred years, we have been aware of precedents in other fields. The federal government uses a loophole to intrude into a field which does not come under its jurisdiction and once its position is established, it seeks to monopolize and take everything.
For years, for one hundred years in fact, Quebec and other provinces have consistently refused to allow the federal government to interfere in the field of education.
Today, by the roundabout way of legislation on broadcasting, the hon. Secretary of State is trying to open a small side window into the wall, in order that the federal government may penetrate in a field whose jurisdiction is exclusively provincial.
One might say that one intended only to provide to the Canadian broadcasting system educational broadcasting facilities. However, Mr. Chairman, Quebec is already working in that direction. Educational broadcasting is already in existence. In the area of Saguenay-Lake St. John, every day, morning and evening, there are educational programs entitled "Quebec-television scolaire", produced by the Quebec government.
The Quebec government already has its own organization in the field of educational programs. It already has its own equipment for educational television and two television stations are already broadcasting, on a trial basis, educational programs. The federal government now wants to venture into that field,

when a provincial government has actually spent money to buy such equipment, which means that the federal government would also like to buy more equipment for exactly the same purpose, thus duplicating our funds and taxes.
In the province of Quebec-and maybe in the others also, I am not quite sure, the matter is perhaps under consideration-such equipment has already been purchased, a committee has been formed to operate it, films have been produced and are broadcast every day, morning and night, on the screens by private television stations in the Sague-nay-Lake St. John area.
The two stations of our area, those of Chicoutimi and Jonquiere, broadcast these films every morning and every night and give courses to those wishing to continue their 7th, 8th, 9th or 10th grades.
It has already started. The expenditures have been made. The equipment has been purchased. Why pay a second time and when it is already there and, furthermore, this is an exclusively provincial jurisdiction. What moves the Secretary of State to spend money to buy a second time what has already been purchased?
Are we also going to train another crew to use this equipment? Mr. Chairman, there is already a crew. It exists, it is there, more advanced than the embryo stage, because it has already started to prove its worth, if we are to judge by what we can see on the television screens.
If it exists, why this duplication? I was told-and I made an effort to see them this morning, also in Ottawa-about educational films prepared by the Ontario department of education which are fine indeed. Naturally, education falls within provincial jurisdiction, and Ontario attends to it. There could be an exchange of French language films between Quebec and Ontario, even though the member for York-Humber (Mr. Cowan) shakes his head. Indeed, English language films could be exchanged by the departments of education of British Columbia, Newfoundland and Ontario.
It is already the case, it has already been paid for once, in the form of taxes. Our taxes paid to the Quebec government have already been used to buy all that, but they would want the Quebec citizens to pay a second time for some equipment which would be placed in another building, which would come under the Ottawa government, another equipment exactly the same as the Quebec equipment, being a duplication thereof.
January 29, 1968

Why, Mr. Chairman? I admit that sometimes-and it is an argument which has been already put forward-the federal government has interfered in certain fields, precisely due to the lack of action by the provincial governments.
When the house passed the hospital insurance scheme, it was said that the provinces had taken no action and that the citizens who could not afford it still had the right to be hospitalized. It was true, the provinces had taken no action.
However, in this case, the provinces have already taken some action. The equipment has already been bought, already paid for and some crews have already been given the responsibility to use that equipment. Professors have already been hired; they have already prepared lectures and the films produced are shown on television. A series of lectures has already started since the beginning of January, I think. They have been shown by the Jonquiere and Chicoutimi television stations. The equipment purchased was tested successfully.
If it has already been bought, the federal government can no longer say that the provinces are taking no action. This argument no longer applies, for Quebec already owns this equipment. So it would be a needless expenditure on the part of the federal government, since it has already been done, and there would be a duplication of taxes for Canadians.
I cannot see why the hon. Secretary of State would want to do that, since the field of education is a provincial matter.
I will be told that the provinces are the ones which will decide how to use the facilities and which will set up their own courses.
I cannot imagine the Quebec government, which is already fully equipped, turning to the C.B.C. and telling them: You have the facilities, we will use them. I cannot imagine the Quebec government wanting to borrow the facilities of the federal government when Quebec already fully controls facilities which a group of competent professors is already using, since they have more experience in that field than the officials of the federal government.
In my opinion, that clause is unnecessary, it is one more infringement of the Canadian constitution, in short it violates the Canadian constitution.
We will be told that nothing will be imposed on us in the field of education. I

Canadian Policy on Broadcasting know the argument of the Secretary of State, but provinces have already complete and very adequate equipment. Why then put at the disposal of a province equipment which has already been purchased and paid for? It is a good argument since Quebec already has such equipment to produce its own school films. The minister can no longer put forward the pretext that it is to purchase equipment which she will make available to provinces, because provinces already have it. Such a reason can no longer be put forward.
What are they trying to hide by introducing such a clause? Would the hon. Secretary of State like the Canadian broadcasting system to have an educational network which would produce its own films? Mr. Chairman, in my opinion this clause is useless both from the constitutional and from the practical point of view. It would perhaps have been useful a year and a half or two years ago, when the provinces had taken no initiative in this field, but not now, when the provinces have taken steps in this respect, bought facilities and acquired experience. In fact, in the province of Quebec, courses are already being telecast, and the hon. members for Roberval and Chicoutimi (Messrs. Gauthier and Langlois) will no doubt bear testimony to this, since they must have seen these courses produced by the province of Quebec, using Quebec equipment and with the help of a team of Quebec professors. Moreover, education falls within the jurisdiction of the province of Quebec.
In my opinion, to spend again some taxpayers' money to purchase equipment already available would be duplication of public funds and this is unacceptable. A second series of programs is perhaps planned.
Mr. Chairman, may I call it ten o'clock.
It being ten o'clock, shall I rise, report progress and request leave to sit again at the next sitting of the house?

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the federal government has undertaken to provide access to Sea island to service the new
[The Assistant Deputy Chairman.!
DEBATES	January 29, 1968
international airport being built by the Department of Transport for Vancouver and the lower British Columbia mainland. The terms and conditions under which the federal government accepted this responsibility were that user charges would be sufficient to recover the capital cost of the facility over a reasonable amortization period. It is not now and never has been the responsibility of the Department of Transport to provide vehicular access to and from crown owned airports.
The government has been of the opinion that it could not logically be expected to provide roadways to airports on a non-toll basis. It must be readily apparent that the capital cost of undertaking such a policy on a national scale would be enormous, especially in major centres such as Montreal and Toronto.
However, in Vancouver we have a rather unique situation. The airport is located on an island that is not now adequately serviced by crossings to meet the demand of the existing airport. It was also made apparent by local municipal authorities that they were not in any position to finance the construction of facilities required to meet existing and future traffic demands expected to be generated by the opening of the new international air terminal later this year.
For these reasons the federal government agreed to construct the necessary facilities to provide adequate access to the new airport on the understanding that tolls, sufficient to recover the capital cost of the facilities over a reasonable number of years, would be levied on the users.
I want to make it quite clear on behalf of the government that the government on the other hand does not intend to levy these tolls against residents of Sea island who have a traditional right of free access to the island. Special arrangements will be made to ensure that anyone who is now resident on the island will not face toll charges to get to and from his residence and place of work.

Mr. Speaker, I am sure the Minister of Trade and Commerce would like me to express his regrets at not being able to be here this evening to listen to the hon. member's very effective submission. As he knows, the minister is away in Europe and Asia on a selling mission, and I am sure we all wish him well. We certainly hope he will be able to sell more wheat during his mission there.
The hon. member for Mackenzie has asked whether there will be a transfer of funds to the Canadian Wheat Board as a result of the recent sale of wheat to China. Perhaps I should repeat the government's guarantee to western grain producers as announced by the Minister of Trade and Commerce to the House of Commons on September 27, as recorded at page 2558 of Hansard:
Pending ratification and only until that date, the government is prepared to make up the difference between the agreed schedule of Geneva minimum prices, related to approximately $1,951 basis
[Mr. Korchinski.)
DEBATES	January 29, 1968
No. 1 Northern in store at the Lakehead, and any wheat sold by the Canadian Wheat Board below this level during the period August 1, 1967 and July 1, 1968.
This means that on any and each sale made by the Canadian Wheat Board between August 1, 1967 and June 30, 1968, at prices under the agreed international grains arrangement minimums, the government will make up the difference to the board. This action was intended to enable the board to price competitively without undermining the per bushel return to producers.
Hon. members are aware that for commercial reasons it has been the long standing practice on the part of the government not to divulge the selling price of wheat in individual markets. I cannot therefore comment on any individual sale by Canada in relation to the minimum prices set out in the new international grain agreement. I can only repeat that the government will reimburse the wheat board for each sale negotiated at a price level under the I.G.A. minimums. The government will shortly be tabling an estimate in the house for this purpose.

Mr. Speaker, I am very pleased to see that a scientist, the parliamentary secretary to the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources, will reply to me when I complete my brief remarks. I may say that I represent a riding which includes several research groups interested in scientific achievements. In these groups we find the very large and competent group of the Consolidated Mining and Smelting Company, the research group in Notre Dame University at Nelson, the research group of Selkirk College at Castlegar, and the group concerned with forest research in the Celgar Corporation in the Castlegar district.
All these groups have followed very closely the developments in the research industry, in government and in universities, and they have followed very closely the development of the intense neutron generator. In this connection I want to quote very briefly from Science Forum, to indicate the importance of this astounding development. I am quoting from an article entitled, "I.N.G.: A vehicle to new frontiers" by L. G. Elliott, W. Bennett
January 29, 1968	COMMONS
Lewis and A. G. Ward, men well known in this field:
Possibly the most contentious issue in Canadian science today is the proposal by Atomic Energy of Canada Limited to build the intense neutron generator. Dispute has arisen primarily because of its high cost (between $150 and $200 million capital cost plus $20 million a year operating cost) and the fear that it will sap government funds away from other areas of science. But there are other issues besides this question of national priorities. Some scientists feel that there has been insufficient discussion of the project, and even that debate has been discouraged. The deans of Canada's engineering schools have expressed concern about I.N.G., but the Science Council of Canada has given its provisional approval. Cabinet approval still is needed before the project can go ahead.
In order to promote discussion of this important issue, Science Forum has sought opinions on both the pros and cons of I.N.G. from its principal proponents and other scientists knowledgeable in several areas-engineering and materials science, nuclear physics and high energy physics. These are presented in this and the following articles. Other aspects are dealt with in the comment section.
The article is a complete analysis of the situation from various points of view. There is another article that deals briefly with the opposing views and it is entitled, "I.N.G.: The wrong thing, in the wrong place, at the wrong time". The article reads in part:
Nevertheless I believe that I.N.G., which is possibly the biggest and certainly the most expensive single undertaking in the history of Canadian scientific research is the wrong thing, in the wrong place, at the wrong time.
The author goes on to give the reasons he has for coming to this conclusion.
Then, I go to another article entitled, "I.N.G.: A good thing-under certain conditions", by K. G. McNeill. He has this to say in part:
There are, then, two very major logistic problems connected with placement and timing. At the moment, only at Chalk River can the initial development be done, but the final location must be elsewhere-somewhere within an easy hour or two of an international airport, a large industrial centre, industrial research laboratories, a number of universities, teaching hospitals, a major arterial road. With respect to timing, it must be built sufficiently swiftly that exciting experiments are not done elsewhere (as they undoubtedly will be in time), but the urgency must not be such that everything is built abroad. Such matters require decision-and I believe one of the worst things that can happen is for a firm decision about the future of I.N.G. to be delayed or not made clear. If that happens we may finally end up, not with an accelerator in hand, but with an accelerator in the bush, which no one by then will really want.
In summary, I believe I.N.G. is good for science, and that with the right conditions it can be good for Canadian science and good for Canada. But I do not see the guarantee of these right conditions in current plans.

The conditions which this gentleman lays down as to the location, point very definitely to the Kootenays as a suitable site for this development. We have an airport there; we have research laboratories, teaching hospitals, universities and all the rest. Mr. Speaker, I should like to address to the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources a question of considerable importance to the people of this country. In view of press reports about the recommendation of the Science Council of Canada that an intense neutron generator be built at a cost of $150 million, and in view of press reports that the federal cabinet has approved the expenditure of $1 million to investigate a site which would provide an ample source of cheap power, what action has been taken on this question to date and has the minister received representations from mayor F. E. DeVito of Trail, on behalf of the regional district, that the Kootenays be considered for this site as being an appropriate one for the development of cheap power-
[DOT] (10:20 p.m.)
The United States is carrying on investigations in this respect in Chicago. Unless we are very careful the United States will be ahead of us in this very unusual and outstanding development. speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I listened with great interest and not a little sympathy to the submission made by the hon. member for Kootenay West. As he well knows, his area, and certainly the Trail area, has been active in the past in nuclear programs. It was the first source-a very efficient and economic source-of heavy water back in the early days of atomic energy in the mid-40's. From some of the things he said and from some of the things I have read I see no reason why his area would not be seriously considered for the location of a big research project of this type.
I.N.G.-the intense neutron generator project-would if undertaken in this country be the largest basic research program Canadians have ever initiated. Its capital cost would be in excess of $150 million and it would have an annual operating budget of $20 million a year. This is big money in anyone's terms.
January 29, 1968

Proceedings on Adjournment Motion
The hon. member said that there had been insufficient discussion of this subject. He derived that statement from the new publication "Science Forum", which I think is an excellent one. The authors of this publication are to be commended for their interest not only in I.N.G., its nature, its pros and cons and its location, but also for their intention of going on to explore other scientific projects, as well.
This publication states that the pros and cons of I.N.G. should be looked into very carefully. I can assure the hon. member that the government is looking into them very carefully. The budget for the coming fiscal year 1968-69 is approximately $1.5 million. Those funds are being devoted to further investigation into the desirability of this project being undertaken over the next six or seven years.
There is also the important matter of logistics-as the "Science Forum" described it-of location as well as timing. The hon. member is quite correct; you do need good transportation facilities and an industrial airport. You also need nearby an industrial complex that is really interested in scientific research so that the scientists can talk to other scientists in related disciplines. You need research laboratories of other types.
It is not clear that the I.N.G. development should be located at Chalk River. It could be located in one of half a dozen other areas in Canada. My understanding is that if this project were to go ahead it would have a high Canadian content-75 per cent or more-and would employ at least 50 top grade scientists.
As I said at the beginning, Mr. Speaker, a big decision is involved. It is a very expensive project, one which can, however, break new ground in a big way in basic research in this country. It is being looked at carefully, and I have mentioned the scale of the budget so as to indicate the government's continuing interest and intent in this regard.

subtopic: BROADCASTING-CORRESPONDENCE RESPECTING PROMOTION OF NATIONAL UNITY

speechtext:
Montreal, Que., November 6, 4:18 P.M.
The Honourable Judy LaMarsh,
Secretary of State,
House of Commons,
Ottawa, Ontario.
Madame, you have recently stated on private and public television that the CBC must be a factor in national unity, and whoever is not ready to conform to this aim should leave the corporation. You are already interpreting the bill on broadcasting in a manner which is most disturbing and which compromises the exercise of our profession. We take objection to the wording in a law which reads: The national broadcasting service should.. .contribute to the strengthening of national unity... We believe that our prime role, as producers, is to reflect and to interpret the living reality in a country. We do not believe that official government thinking is necessarily the kind of objective thinking which should be the basis of political and cultural information. The CBC is obliged to bring to light all forms of power in the sense that it must allow a confrontation of forces and debates on the relative values of any given society. If we are to be the vehicle for or to promote one political line then we are willingly conniving with an organ of propaganda. We have at all times refused to do so; we refuse to do so today, when what you are saying is in short, that the Left will be tolerated on the condition that it be reactionary. And in this way our function as producers will remain while governments come and go. And thus will it be as long as "Ici Radio Canada" and "This is the CBC network" are heard by Quebeckers, "Canadiens" and "Canadians".
The Association of Producers
Claude Sylvestre, Secretary
P.S. The Association includes CBC television producers in Montreal, Quebec, Ottawa, Halifax, Cornerbrook, St. Johns (Newfoundland), Winnipeg, Edmonton, Vancouver. For the promotion of the interests of "Canadiens" and "Canadians".
THE SECRETARY OF STATE Canada

Ottawa, November 10, 1967 Dear Mr. Sylvestre,
I have your telegram of November 6 on behalf of the Association of Producers.
Let me first offer the reassurance, if such is required, that there is nothing in the Broadcasting Act nor is there any intention on the part of the government to in any way interfere with the fundamental right of Canadians, whether CBC employees or otherwise, to hold personal and private political views of their own choosing. The issue then is solely in terms of the responsibilities of CBC employees as, in a very real sense, the custodians of a powerful and valuable national asset provided and supported by the people of Canada.
I trust that I am interpreting your telegram correctly in thinking that we are agreed, too, that no CBC employee has the right to use these facilities entrusted to him as a vehicle for promulgating his own political viewpoint, no matter what that might be. Nor has any employee the right to use these facilities in a manner subversive to the democratic process.
As for your role in positive terms, I support, and I believe the legislation supports, your own interpretation that it is "to reflect and to interpret the living reality in a country." I accept that statement, provided you mean by "reflect" an honest attempt to mirror the broad spectrum of Canadian viewpoints, and by "interpret" an honest effort to present and explain these viewpoints with balance and perspective.
Nor can I take any objection nor find any in the legislation to your thesis that the CBC should not be "an organ of propaganda" in promoting particular political policies or points of view of any government, party, movement or indeed of any individual.
The Corporation does have a definite right, indeed an obligation, to ensure that these various policies and points of view are exposed to the Canadian people. But the decision as to which proposals are to be implemented rests surely with the people who, forming their judgments on the basis of the

January 29, 1968
varied information available from the CBC and other media, express their will through their legislatures and their governments. The Corporation's mandate, in short, is to expose problems and identify options for the people, in a fair and balanced way, but not to dictate solutions or choices to them.
The question then is whether Section 2 (g) (iv) in the Broadcasting Act, in fact, infringes either on the essential independence of the Corporation from particular political policies and pressures or on the equally fundamental requirement that the citizens of Canada have available to them through the CBC a comprehensive and balanced exposition of all available viewpoints.
I think one must look for the answer to this question first and foremost among the reasons why we have a Canadian Broadcasting Corporation, why it was decided in 1932 to establish a publicly-owned broadcasting system and why that system has been supported and re-enforced by succeeding Parliaments continuously since that time. Let me refer to but two of the statements which the then-Prime Minister, R. B. Bennett, made in introducing the legislation in question:
"Canadians have the right to a system of broadcasting from Canadian sources equal in all respects to that of any other country. The enormous benefits of an adequate scheme of radio broadcasting controlled and operated by Canadians are abundantly plain. Properly employed radio can be a most effective instrument in nation-building with an educational value difficult to estimate."
And again:
"First of all, this country must be assured of complete control of broadcasting from Canadian sources, free from foreign interference or influence. Without such control radio broadcasting can never become a great agency for the communication of matters of national concern and for the diffusion of national thought and ideals and without such control it can never be the agency by which national consciousness may be fostered and sustained and national unity still further strengthened."
The underlining is, of course, mine-to stress the most fundamental fact!-the CBC was created, and has been maintained since, not as an agency independent or neutral from Canadian unity, but precisely to foster and enrich that unity. Or, to use the words of Bill 163-C, "to contribute to the strengthening of national unity."
Certainly the CBC is independent of government. As you so aptly put it, its function remains "as governments come and go." But the CBC never has been and is not now independent from Canada, from the existence of this country as a single sovereign state. In truth, the Corporation draws its own existence from the very fact of Canada.
That does not mean, of course, that the CBC is bound by the concepts of national unity laid down by Mr. Bennett in 1932 or by any other government, past or present. Surely the applicable concept or form of national unity at any point in time is precisely what the people of Canada at that point in time want it to be for that point in time. If the process of nation-building is never ending, so certainly the political arrangements of a single unified state are not bound in time or cement.
As I have noted previously, we agree that the CBC has a right and obligation to contribute to that process by, in your own words, reflecting and interpreting the various viewpoints available at any particular time concerning these arrangements. But in meeting this responsibility, the CBC must act within the bounds of its overall mandate to contribute to the development, not the destruction, of our national unity, whatever particular form the people of Canada might will for it at any given point in our history.
In that context and in those terms, I find nothing in the new broadcasting legislation to contradict the role of CBC producers as you yourselves envisage your professional responsibilities.
Sincerely,
Judy LaMarsh.
Tuesday, January 30, 1963
